doc.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: New York studio and TV work
title: Paul Simon's session and playing bass guitar on The Tonight Show
summary: Simon wanted straight eighth notes the guitarists could not play; later Pizzarelli played six-string bass for Simon and Garfunkel.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Well we were on a session, I’ll never forget, I know it was Tony Mottola playing guitar and Sol Gubin was playing drums, and a couple of other guitar players. And it was Paul Simon, believe me. And he kept saying I don’t like what I’m hearing from the guitars. And he picked up one of our guitars and played these eighth notes like you described, and that’s the feel he wanted, but none of us knew how to do it. But he had that in his mind way back when he first started. I don’t think these records ever came out but they might be in the can yet at MGM.
Yeah he actually had his first duo, it was called Tom and Jerry I think, and he didn’t really make it at that point, maybe that’s what you were talking about.

I actually played with him once, I had forgotten, I had played with so many different people that I had made a record with him and he was a guest on The Tonight Show with Garfunkel. I got a call, I was home, and they said we need a bass guitar and you’re the one that made the record or something. So I had to race in play that one number with them.
On the bass guitar, but it was a six string bass guitar. It was an octave lower than the regular guitar, and it doubled the string bass.
Wow. I love listening to the difference in the way they recorded things back then too, in that the bass wasn’t nearly as prominent as in pop music nowadays.
Oh yeah. It finally got to that Fender bass and it got too loud, I mean for me, I never liked that.
